title: EXAMINATION: P2F (W01814039)
text:
OPERATIONS DEPARTMENT
M123
Decision on the inherent distinctiveness of an International registration
designating the European Union (Article 7 and Article 182 EUTMR)
Alicante, 30/07/2026
LKGLOBAL Partnerschaftsgesellschaft mbB
Brienner Str. 11
D-80333 München
ALEMANIA
Your reference: 2023 23 86 83 (EggjkQqlxdz/Uc+A)
International registration No: 1814039
Trade Mark: P2F
Name of the holder: Elbe Flugzeugwerke GmbH
Grenzstraße 1
01109 Dresden
Germany
I. Summary of the facts
On 07/07/2025 the Office issued a Notification of ex officio provisional refusal of protection
pursuant to Article 7(1)(b) and (c) and Article 7(2) EUTMR because it found that the trade
mark applied for is descriptive and devoid of any distinctive character.
The goods and services for which the provisional refusal was issued were:
Class 12 Apparatus for locomotion by air; aircraft; aeroplanes; aeronautical apparatus,
machines and appliances; airplanes and structural parts therefor; aircraft
components, included in this class; airplanes and structural parts therefor;
structural parts for aircraft; fuselages of aircraft; structural and non-structural
lightweight panels for aircraft; honeycomb composite panels for aircraft;
lightweight components in the structure and interior of aircraft, in particular flat
lightweight components; fittings for vehicle conversions, namely structural
fittings for aircraft cabins, in particular floor panels, cargo hold floor panels,
linings, partitions for aircraft, vehicle partitions, partitions for aircraft cabins,
structural cabin fittings; cabin linings for aircraft, ceiling panels; vehicle doors,
in particular cockpit doors; cargo hold panels; aircraft tail lifts.
Class 37 Installation, maintenance, servicing, overhaul, conversion and repair, and
disassembly and reassembly of vehicles, in particular vehicles and apparatus
for locomotion by land, air or water, in particular aeroplanes; maintenance
and repair of cargo holds; aircraft repair work; aircraft repair and
maintenance; repair services in the field of computer hardware, aircraft
instruments and aircraft maintenance tools; installation work in the field of the
aeronautical industry; aircraft structural modifications and structural repairs;
Avenida de Europa, 4 • E - 03008 • Alicante, Spain
Tel. +34 965139100 • www.euipo.europa.eu

Page 2 of 11
advice on aircraft repairs and maintenance; provision of information relating to
maintenance and repair; organization of maintenance and repair of aircraft;
providing information on repair services in the aviation sector; maintenance,
servicing, overhaul and repair of components and accessories for aircraft;
installation and expansion of components and accessories in aircraft;
modification of motor vehicles, in particular aircraft; modifications to the
structure, cockpit and avionics of aircraft; modifications of the cabin;
conversion at aeroplanes, in particular conversion of passenger aircraft into
cargo aircraft, assembly and construction of aircraft; modification of aircraft;
conversion of aircraft; organization of maintenance and repair; modifications
to aircraft structure.
Class 42 Providing scientific advice related to aircraft engineering; technical
consultancy, appraisal, testing and monitoring in the technological field, in
particular relating to transport; research and technical consultancy in the field
of aeronautics; aircraft engineering; design, development, construction
planning, configuration and construction planning of aircraft, in particular
aircraft components; provision of technical operating data for aircraft;
technological services in the field of flight simulation; technical flight tests;
aircraft design; development of aircraft; furnishing design services for the
interiors of aircraft; development of flat lightweight components for structure
and interior, in particular fiber-reinforced flat sandwich panels for structure
and interior; technical research in the field of aeronautics; testing, analysis
and evaluation of goods and services for third parties for certification and
approval purposes, in particular for aircraft conversions; certification and
approval activities, in particular for aircraft components; technical advice on
organizational approval when planning aircraft and on processes and
procedures in aircraft development.
The grounds for refusal were based on the following main findings:
• This provisional refusal was sent in order to provide further clarification regarding the
topics raised in the provisional refusal of 12/11/2024, including the objection of
additional goods and services.
• How descriptiveness is assessed depends on how the relevant consumer would
perceive the sign in relation to the goods and services for which protection is sought.
In this case, the relevant English-speaking consumer, namely a professional in the
field of aviation and aircraft engineering and conversion would understand the sign
as having the following meaning: Passenger to Freighter.
• The abovementioned meaning of the word ‘P2F’, of which the trade mark consists,
was supported by the internet references included in the following links (information
extracted on 04/07/2025).
- https://www.stattimes.com/air-cargo/p2f-conversions-is-it-a-game-changer-for-
the-air-cargo-industry-1352925
- https://www.aviationbusinessnews.com/cargo/new-freighters-vs-passenger-to-
freighter-conversions/
- https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/p2f-experts-review-the-current-state-of-the-
market-and-whats-ahead
The relevant content of these links was reproduced in the Notification of ex officio
provisional refusal of protection.

Page 3 of 11
• Taking into account that all the objected goods and services in Classes 12, 37 and
42 have a common feature, namely that they are airplanes / are related to airplanes
(or airplane industry), it is likely that consumers would perceive the sign as providing
information that all those goods and services are airplanes that originally were
passenger aircraft and have been converted into cargo aircrafts or are aimed to
convert airplanes that originally were passenger aircraft and have been converted
into cargo aircrafts. Therefore, the sign will be perceived as describing the nature and
purpose of part of the goods and services for which protection is sought and not as a
trade mark.
• Given that the sign has a clear descriptive meaning, it is also devoid of any distinctive
character and therefore ineligible for registration under Article 7(1)(b) EUTMR. This
means that it is incapable of performing the essential function of a trade mark, which
is to distinguish the goods or services of one undertaking from those of other
undertakings.
• Furthermore, the Office considers that the relevant public would simply perceive the
sign ‘P2F’ as a non-distinctive indication conveying that the goods and services
applied for are related to passenger aircraft that have been converted into cargo
aircrafts. Indeed and as it has been demonstrated above, the expression ‘P2F’ it is
commonly used in a non-distinctive way in relation to the airplane industry.
Therefore, the Office considers it unlikely that consumers perceive the mark as a
distinctive expression.
• Consequently, taken as a whole, the sign is descriptive and devoid of distinctive
character. It is therefore incapable of distinguishing the goods and services for which
an objection has been raised under Article 7(1)(b) and (c) and Article 7(2) EUTMR.
II. Summary of the holder’s arguments
The holder submitted its observations on 17/03/2025 (in reply to the Notification of ex officio
provisional refusal of protection of 12/11/2024) and on 07/11/2025 (in reply to the Notification
of ex officio provisional refusal of protection of 07/07/2025), which may be summarised as
follows:
• The shareholders of the holder are AIRBUS and ST Engineering, and all references
to the term ‘P2F’ that predate the filing date of the trademark go back to those
companies (Company | Elbe Flugzeugwerke GmbH). This is also the case with the
references you cited, which explicitly refer to AIRBUS. The letter combination P2F
goes back to the holder and with this application it would like to prevent it from
becoming a generic term.
• The German PTO initially objected an identical mark, but later it lifted the objection
following the holder’s explanations.
• The holder makes an introduction about its business, including different evidence
about this business and the trade mark ‘P2F’. In particular the evidence submitted is
the following:
- Exhibit JBR1.- Approval of incorporation from the Economics Ministry.
- Exhibit JBR2.- Historical company register extract.
- Exhibit JBR3.- Chronological register extract.
- Exhibit JBR4.- Holder’s registration certificated (HRB 1378).

Page 4 of 11
- Exhibit JBR5.- Details of the holder’s activities.
- Exhibit JBR6.- Details of the holder’s activities.
- Exhibit JBR7.- Extracts from EADS EFW GmbH’s financial statements 2009 and
2010 (page 1).
- Exhibit JBR8.- Extracts from EADS EFW GmbH’s financial statements 2009 and
2010 (page 14).
- Exhibit JBR9.- Extracts from EADS EFW GmbH’s financial statements 2011
(page 3).
- Exhibit JBR10.- Details about the holder’s leadership in conversion customers in
the e-commerce, express and general cargo sectors.
- Exhibit JBR11.- Web articles demonstrating that the holder is the only
conversion house using the mark to offer its’ goods and services.
- Exhibit JBR12.- Article related partnership between the holder and DHL.
- Exhibit JBR13.- Article related deliver of fourteenth Airbus A330-300 by the
holder to DHL.
- Exhibit JBR14.- Article that confirms that the holder completed its redelivery of
its fourth Airbus A321 freight aircraft (the A321P2F) to Titan Airways.
- Exhibit JBR15.- Reference to the website elbeflugzeugwerke.com.
- Exhibit JBR16.- Web archive that demonstrates that the website was launched
in 2016.
- Exhibit JBR17.- Analytics from etracker.
- Exhibit JBR18.- Extract from STAT Times dated January 2011.
- Exhibit JBR19.- Article from Aircraft Technology Issue 118, published in July
2012.
- Exhibit JBR20.- Article from Airfinance Annual 2013.
- Exhibit JBR21.- Extracts from presentations and pictures from trade fairs.
• The holder reiterates that is the only company that uses the abbreviation ‘P2F’ for the
contested goods and services.
• A minimum degree of distinctive character is sufficient to render Article 7(1)(b)
EUTMR inapplicable. Registration of a sign as a trade mark is not subject to a finding
of a specific level of artistic creativity or imaginativeness on the part of the proprietor
of the trade mark.
• Abbreviations of descriptive terms are themselves descriptive when used in that way
and the relevant public – whether general or specialised – recognises them as
identical to the descriptive meaning of the full word.
• Insofar as the sign P2F can be found in connection with aircraft conversion, these
acts of use can be traced back to the holder. ‘P2F’ is not descriptive in relation to the
goods and services claimed. Rather, several steps of reasoning are required to
establish a descriptive meaning in relation to aircraft. No descriptive connection in
relation to the services claimed can be inferred from the references submitted.
• The content of the first two articles provided by the Office is not available. As regards
the third article, dates from 03/02/2024, after registration of the trade mark in dispute.
The holder confirmed on 02/04/2026 that all the evidence submitted 07/11/2025 was related
to an acquired distinctiveness claim, that should be analyzed as subsidiary.
Taking the above into account, the Office will only analyze in this decision the inherent
distinctiveness of the mark.

Page 5 of 11
III. Reasons
Pursuant to Article 94 EUTMR, it is up to the Office to take a decision based on reasons or
evidence on which the holder has had an opportunity to present its comments.
After giving due consideration to the holder's arguments, the Office has decided to maintain
the grounds for refusal.
Under Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR, ‘trade marks which consist exclusively of signs or indications
which may serve, in trade, to designate the kind, quality, quantity, intended purpose, value,
geographical origin or the time of production of the goods or of rendering of the service, or
other characteristics of the goods or service’ are not to be registered.
It is settled case-law that each of the grounds for refusal to register listed in Article 7(1)
EUTMR is independent and requires separate examination. Moreover, it is appropriate to
interpret those grounds for refusal in the light of the general interest underlying each of them.
The general interest to be taken into consideration must reflect different considerations
according to the ground for refusal in question (16/09/2004, C-329/02 P, SAT.2,
EU:C:2004:532, § 25).
Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR pursues an aim in the public interest, namely that descriptive signs or
indications relating to the characteristics of the goods in respect of which registration is
sought may be freely used by all. This provision does not permit these signs or indications to
be reserved for use by one undertaking as a result of their registration as a trade mark
(04/05/1999, C-108/97 & C-109/97, Chiemsee, EU:C:1999:230, § 25; 27/02/2002, T-219/00,
Ellos, EU:T:2002:44, § 27; 08/04/2003, C-53/01, C-54/01 & C-55/01, Linde, EU:C:2003:206,
§ 73; 06/05/2003, C-104/01, Libertel, EU:C:2003:244, § 52; 12/02/2004, C-265/00, Biomild,
EU:C:2004:87, § 35, 36; 27/04/2016, T-89/15, NIAGARA, EU:T:2016:244, § 12).
The signs or indications that may serve, in trade, to designate characteristics of the goods or
services in respect of which registration is sought are, by virtue of Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR,
regarded as incapable of performing the essential function of a trade mark, namely that of
identifying the commercial origin of the goods or services, therefore enabling the consumer
who acquired the goods or services designated by the mark to repeat the experience if it
proves to be positive, or to avoid it if it proves to be negative, on the occasion of a
subsequent acquisition (23/10/2003, C-191/01 P, Doublemint, EU:C:2003:579, § 30;
27/02/2002, T-219/00, Ellos, EU:T:2002:44, § 28, 27/04/2016, T-89/15, NIAGARA,
EU:T:2016:244, § 12).
Furthermore, Article 7(2) EUTMR states that a trade mark shall not be registered, even if the
grounds of non-registrability are met only in part of the European Union. An obstacle
pertaining to the English-speaking population of the European Union is consequently
sufficient to reject the trade mark application. This primarily consists of consumers in Ireland
and Malta.
The sign’s descriptiveness must be assessed in relation to the goods and services for which
registration is sought and by reference to the relevant public’s perception of it (02/04/2008,
T-181/07, Steadycontrol, EU:T:2008:86, § 38; 21/05/2008, T-329/06, E, EU:T:2008:161,
§ 23).
A trade mark that is descriptive in relation to goods and services in respect of which
registration is sought, it is necessarily devoid of any distinctive character for those goods and
services within the meaning of Article 7(1)(b) EUTMR (12/02/2004, C-363/99, Postkantoor,
EU:C:2004:86, § 86; 14/06/2007, T-207/06, Europig, EU:T:2007:179, § 47).

Page 6 of 11
As demonstrated below, the Office's conclusions regarding the descriptive nature and lack of
distinctive character of the trade mark ‘P2F’ remain unaffected by the holder's arguments.
1. Descriptive character of ‘P2F’
As a preliminary point, the Office refers to the evidence used to demonstrate the descriptive
character of the trade mark ‘P2F’. In particular, the Office refers to the evidence included in
the Notification of ex officio provisional refusal of protection dated 07/07/2025. In that
notification, three screenshots with the corresponding links were included.
With regard to those links, the Office first refers to:
- https://aviationbusinessnews.com/cargo/new-freighters-vs-passenger-to-
freighter-conversions/:
As can be seen from the full screenshot provided above, the article is dated 31/07/2023, that
is to say, almost three months before the International Registration was registered and the
EUIPO was designated by the holder. The article includes the following statement:

Page 7 of 11
Meanwhile, annual passenger-to-freighter (P2F) conversions have reached
historic highs with volume estimated to peak at 180 per year by 2025, and then settle
at around 160 aircraft per year. This compares to 70 units per year before the Covid-
19 pandemic.
This reference is significant not only because it demonstrates the descriptive character of the
expression ‘P2F’, but also because it refers to data predating the COVID-19 pandemic,
which occurred in 2020. Finally and contrary to the holder’s assertions, the article is fully
accessible.
A similar conclusion can be drawn in relation to the article entitled “P2F conversions: Is it a
game changer for the air cargo industry?”, available at: https://www.stattimes.com/air-
cargo/p2f-conversions-is-it-a-game-changer-for-the-air-cargo-industry-1352925 (which,
contrary to the holder’s assertions, is fully accessible), where the following is stated:
In fact, the rising curve for air cargo demand is going nowhere. In the wake of COVID
19 pandemic when people stopped travelled and started transporting more parcel, be
it the life-saving drugs, vaccines or e-commerce parcels, air cargo sector saw a
massive boost. As a result, a lot of new players in the P2F conversions was born.
For instance, Mammoth Freighters was established in 2020 while Kansas
Modification Center (KMC) was founded in 2021.
In this instance as well, reference is made to the COVID-19 pandemic and to companies that
commenced operations in this sector in 2020 and 2021.
Finally, the last article https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/p2f-experts-review-the-current-
state-of-the-market-and-whats-ahead, also refers to the descriptive meaning of ‘P2F’ and to
the Covid-19 pandemic:
In the Office’s view, the evidence provided clearly demonstrates that the expression ‘P2F’
was descriptive and lacked distinctive character in relation to the contested goods and

Page 8 of 11
services prior to the filing date of the trade mark.
In this regard, and as complementary evidence to that already submitted during the present
proceedings, the Office also refers to the following articles:
- https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/chinas-comac-arj21-passenger-to-freighter-
conversion-program-given-green-light
- https://www.aerotime.aero/articles/32487-embraer-nac-firm-order-e190-e195-
freighter-conversion
Taking into account all the arguments set out above, the Office considers that the descriptive
character of the expression ‘P2F’ is indisputable in the present case, as it refers to
‘Passenger to Freighter’.

Page 9 of 11
Given that all the goods and services applied for are aircraft or are related to aircraft (or to
the aviation industry), the descriptive message conveyed to the relevant consumers is clear
and direct. It informs them that those goods and services concern aircraft that were originally
passenger aircraft and have been converted into cargo aircraft or are intended for such
conversion.
The Office further recalls that the application of Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR does not require that
the sign applied for be understood in a relevant part of the EU from the point of view of the
relevant public. It is instead sufficient if an understanding as a relevant descriptive
indication exists in the minds of a part of the public targeted that is not negligible (cf.
21/06/2017, T-856/16, LONGHORN STEAKHOUSE, EU:T:2017:412, § 30; 04/05/2022, T-
261/21, Steaker, EU:T:2022:269, § 30 et. seq.).
Furthermore, and contrary to the holder’s arguments, no mental effort is required to conclude
that ‘P2F’ would be perceived as a descriptive term in relation to the contested goods and
services. It should be borne in mind that the relevant public consists of professionals in the
field of aviation and aircraft engineering and conversion, who are accustomed to
encountering ‘P2F’ used in the manner described by the Office. This conclusion is
particularly important given that the decisive factor is not an abstract understanding of the
sign, but rather the perception of the sign by the relevant public in the context of the
goods and services applied for (09/07/2008, T-304/06, Mozart, EU:T:2008:268, § 103;
09/03/2010, T-77/09, Nature watch, EU:T:2010:81, § 26).
In light of the above, the Office considers that the holder’s arguments are not conclusive and
maintains the objection based on Article 7(1)(c) EUTMR.
2. Lack of distinctiveness of ‘P2F’
As the Office has demonstrated above, ‘P2F’ is descriptive in relation to the contested goods
and services and, therefore, it is necessarily devoid of any distinctiveness for those goods
within the meaning of Article 7(1)(b) EUTMR (12/02/2004, C-363/99, Postkantoor,
EU:C:2004:86, § 86; 14/06/2007, T-207/06, Europig, EU:T:2007:179, § 47).
Furthermore, the Office has concluded that the relevant public would simply perceive the
sign ‘P2F’ as a non-distinctive indication conveying that the goods and services applied for
are related to passenger aircraft that have been converted into cargo aircraft. As explained
above, the expression ‘P2F’ is commonly used in a non-distinctive manner in the aviation
industry. Therefore, it is unlikely that consumers would perceive the mark as a distinctive
indication of commercial origin.
In this regard, the Office refers to the decision of the 1st Board of Appeal of 23/06/2026 in
Case R 1934/2025-1, NCA, in which the Board stated:
In that regard, the Board observes that, while the acronymic form of a sign does
not in itself justify a refusal, a short combination of letters that is devoid of any
semantic or imaginative content of its own and that coincides, in the relevant
field, with an established abbreviation or technical code is perceived by the
relevant public as that code rather than as an associative link with a
specific commercial origin. In the present case, the sign ‘NCA’ does not
display any element that would enable the relevant public to depart from such a
technical reading and to perceive it instead as a badge of origin.

Page 10 of 11
The holder also argued that the registration of a trade mark is not subject to any requirement
of linguistic or artistic creativity. While this is correct, in the present case the mark contains
no additional element capable of supporting the conclusion that the expression ‘P2F’ is
unusual or original, particularly in relation to the goods and services concerned.
On the other hand, the Office acknowledges the holder’s arguments concerning the
minimum degree of distinctive character of the contested mark.
However, in the present case there is not even a small degree of distinctiveness of whatever
kind (see 19/09/2002, C-104/00 P, Companyline, EU:C:2002:506, § 20; 30/04/2015, T-
707/13, BE HAPPY, EU:T:2015:252, § 47). Moreover, account should be taken that not only
signs which have ‘not even a minimum degree of distinctiveness’ must be refused, but all
signs devoid of any distinctive character and not only those which are obviously not
eligible for protection. Examination of absolute grounds of refusal must be carried out
thoroughly and in full and cannot be limited to a ‘minimum degree’ (12/02/2004, C-
363/99, Postkantoor, EU:C:2004:86, § 123, 125).
It follows from consistent case-law, that a finding of a lack of distinctiveness may be lawfully
based on matters of common knowledge arising from practical experience generally
acquired from the marketing of general consumer goods or services, without specific
examples having to be provided (10/11/2004, T-402/02, Bonbonverpackung, EU:T:2004:330,
§ 58; 22/06/2006, C-25/05 P, Bonbonverpackung, EU:C:2006:422, § 54; 15/03/2006,
T-129/04, Plastikflaschenform, EU:T:2006:84, § 19).
It is on the basis of that acquired experience that the Office submits that the relevant
consumers will perceive the sign as ordinary and not as the trade mark of a particular
proprietor. Since the holder claimed that the sign is distinctive, despite the Office’s analysis
based on the abovementioned experience, it is up to the holder to provide specific and
substantiated information to show that the sign is distinctive, either intrinsically or acquired
through use, since it is much better placed to do so, given its thorough knowledge of the
market (05/03/2003, T-194/01, Soap device, EU:T:2003:53, § 48).
As no conclusive evidence or arguments have been submitted by the holder to demonstrate
the distinctiveness of the term ‘P2F’, the Office also maintains the objection under Article
7(1)(b) EUTMR.
3. Previous registration in the Germany
Finally, the holder refers to an identical trade mark that allegedly was registered in Germany.
However, this registration cannot be considered by the Office given that, in this particular
case, the relevant language is English and not German. Moreover, the Office would like to
remind that, according to established case-law:
the European Union trade mark regime is an autonomous system with its own
set of objectives and rules peculiar to it; it is self-sufficient and applies
independently of any national system … Consequently, the registrability of a
sign as a European Union trade mark must be assessed by reference only to
the relevant Union rules. Accordingly, the Office and, if appropriate, the Union
judicature are not bound by a decision given in a Member State, or indeed a
third country, that the sign in question is registrable as a national mark. That is
so even if such a decision was adopted under national legislation harmonised
with Directive 89/104 or in a country belonging to the linguistic area in which the
word sign in question originated.

Page 11 of 11
(27/02/2002, T-106/00, STREAMSERVE, EU:T:2002:43, § 47).
In light of the above, the holder’s arguments in relation to a previous registration in the
Germany should also be set aside.
IV. Conclusion
For the abovementioned reasons, and pursuant to Article 7(1)(b) and (c) and Article 7(2)
EUTMR the International Registration No W01814039 designating the European Union is
declared to be descriptive and non-distinctive in the English-speaking territories of the
European Union, namely Ireland and Malta for all the goods and services claimed.
According to Article 66(2) EUTMR, you have a right to appeal against this decision which
does not terminate the examination proceedings. According to Article 68 EUTMR, notice of
appeal must be filed in writing at the Office within two months of the date of notification of
this decision. It must be filed in the language of the proceedings in which the decision
subject to appeal was taken. Furthermore, a written statement of the grounds for appeal
must be filed within four months of the same date. The notice of appeal will be deemed to
have been filed only when the appeal fee of EUR 720 has been paid.
Once this decision has become final, the proceedings will be resumed for the examination of
the subsidiary claim based upon Article 7(3) EUTMR and Article 2(2) EUTMIR.
Pablo AMAT RODRÍGUEZ
